title: Why the author wrote it
keyIdea: Every text has an author's purpose: to persuade you, to inform you, or to entertain you. Push words such as should, must and best show an author is persuading, even when the text also uses facts. The author's point of view is what the author thinks; your own view can be different. Loaded words show the author's attitude, and you prove a purpose by pointing to the words that show it.

kid: Every text has a reason. Authors write to persuade you, to inform you, or to entertain you. That reason is called the author's purpose.
To persuade is to make you think or do something. Look for push words like should, must and best. An advert says: You must try it! Persuaders often add facts to make their case stronger.
To inform is to teach you true facts, like how owls hunt. To entertain is to give you a story or a joke to enjoy.

The author's point of view is what the author thinks. You do not have to agree. You can say: The author thinks school should start later, but I think it should not. Words show how the author feels: wasted money sounds cross, spent money sounds calm.
adult: Identifying the author's purpose is a core reading-comprehension standard: US Common Core RI.2.6 asks children to identify the main purpose of a text, and RI.3.6 asks them to distinguish their own point of view from that of the author. The English national curriculum for Years 3 to 6 adds distinguishing statements of fact from opinion and explaining how language contributes to meaning.

Teachers often use the shorthand PIE: persuade, inform, entertain. Informational texts usually inform, adverts and letters to the editor persuade, and stories and poems entertain, but form is only a clue. The best evidence is the language: imperatives, 'should' and 'must', and superlatives signal persuasion.

Common mistakes: deciding that any text with facts must be informing (persuaders use facts as evidence); thinking that a fun or colourful text must be entertaining when it is selling something; believing that disagreeing with the author means you read it wrong; and naming a purpose without quoting the words that show it.

Attitude is shown through word choice. 'The council wasted money' and 'The council invested money' report the same fact, but the loaded verb tells you which side the author is on. Ask your child to swap one word and say how the author now seems to feel.

familyTip: Pick up any leaflet, cereal box or news headline at home. Ask: Why was this written? Which words tell you? Then ask what your child thinks, and let them disagree with the author.

visual.caption: Why was each text written? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: You must try our new pizza!
Vote for a longer lunch break!
The Moon goes round the Earth.
The cat wore boots and sang.
A giant sneezed and the town flew away.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort texts by purpose, find push words, pin your view and the author's, swap loaded words, and prove each purpose.

practice.prompt: "Get your tickets now! It is the best show in town!" Why was it written?
practice.hint: Does it push you to do something? Look for now and best.
practice.explain: "Get your tickets now" tells you what to do and "best" praises the show, so the author wants to persuade you.

practice.prompt: A fact book says a blue whale can be {n} metres long. Why was it written?
practice.hint: Is it teaching you a true fact, or asking you to do something?
practice.explain: A length of {n} metres is a true fact that teaches you about whales. The author wants to inform.

practice.prompt: An advert says: "{n} out of 10 kids love Zoom Shoes. Buy yours today!" What is the purpose?
choices: To persuade, using a fact as help
To inform, because it has a number
To entertain, because it is fun
practice.hint: Find the push words. Is the number there to teach you, or to make you buy?
practice.explain: "Buy yours today" pushes you. The fact that {n} out of 10 kids love them is there to make the push stronger.

practice.prompt: The author thinks dogs make the best pets. You like cats more. What is true?
choices: Your view and the author's view can be different
You must agree with the author
practice.hint: Does a reader have to think the same as the author?
practice.explain: The author's point of view is what the author thinks. You can disagree: the author thinks dogs are best, but I think cats are.

pool.prompt: Which word is a push word that shows persuading?
pool.hint: Which word tells someone what to do?
pool.explain: "Should" tells you what to do, so it is a push word. River and Monday just name things.

pool.prompt: "A dragon ate the king's hat and burped out a rainbow." Why was it written?
pool.hint: Is it true? Is anyone asked to do something?
pool.explain: It is a silly, made-up story with no facts and no push words, so it was written to entertain.

pool.prompt: "The school wasted {n} pounds on new paint." How does the author feel?
pool.hint: Look at the word wasted. Is it a happy or a cross word?
pool.explain: "Wasted" shows the author thinks the {n} pounds were spent badly. They are against it.

pool.prompt: You think the author's purpose is to persuade. How do you prove it?
choices: Point to the push words in the text
pool.hint: Proof comes from the words the author wrote.
pool.explain: Point to words like "you must" or "best ever". The text itself is your evidence.

pool.prompt: A poster says the zoo has {n} animals and you should visit this summer. What is the main purpose?
pool.hint: The number is a fact, but what does the poster want you to do?
pool.explain: "You should visit" is a push. The {n} animals are a fact used to persuade you to go.

pool.prompt: What is the author's point of view?
choices: What the author thinks about the topic
The page the author wrote on
pool.explain: Point of view is what the author thinks. Readers can have a different view of their own.

pool.prompt: "Penguins cannot fly, but they swim very fast." Why was it written?
pool.hint: Is it true? Does it ask you to do anything?
pool.explain: It gives true facts about penguins and asks nothing of you, so the author wants to inform.
